entries.expanded_text: In the years that reshaped the Quilrin, held by the Twin Banners, the question was never whether power would change hands but only which hands would receive it and on what terms. The Twin Banners moved carefully in the Quilrin, replacing key appointments before announcing any broader intention. By the time the shift was publicly visible, it had already been accomplished in every practical sense. The Twin Banners had remade the Quilrin in its own image — or close enough that the difference would only become apparent to those who lived there long enough to notice what had quietly vanished.

entries.expanded_text: In the years that concern us here, the Pelstead, held by the Northwind Host remained dangerously unstable and largely outside the current of larger events. Trade moved through the Pelstead at its customary pace. The ledgers from this era show neither the surpluses of a prosperous season nor the shortfalls that might prompt inquiry from above. In this, the Pelstead was useful — not as a subject of history, but as a foundation beneath it.

entries.expanded_text: Those who had known the Pelstead in better times returned to find it not ruined, exactly, but diminished — as a fire is diminished when the wood runs low. The roads of the Pelstead were the first to show it — maintained, then merely passable, then quietly abandoned to the encroachment of grass and mud. No edict marked the change. It simply happened. Later administrations would attempt revivals of the Pelstead — some earnest, some merely rhetorical. None recovered what the long erosion had taken, because erosion does not leave the original shape intact beneath its work.

entries.expanded_text: In a matter of days, the Zankeld, held by the Lantern Guild continued largely as it had — administered, taxed, and otherwise undisturbed. The Zankeld appears in the dispatch records of this period only in inventory summaries and routine census figures. No military movements were logged. No factional complaints were forwarded. What the Zankeld offered during this period was continuity. Whether that continuity would prove a foundation or merely a pause remained, for now, an open question.

entries.expanded_text: A generation passed quietly over the Greyshore, held by the Ashen League, and when it lifted, the land beneath was measurably different from the land it had covered. The fields and storehouses of the Greyshore did not overflow, but they did not fall short either. That equilibrium, modest as it sounds, was the foundation on which everything else in this period was built. The quiet growth of the Greyshore in these years would not find its way into songs or speeches. It would find its way, instead, into the improved circumstances of those who came after.

entries.expanded_text: In the years that followed, the Windward Marches, held by the Dominion did what stable ground eventually does — it began, without ceremony, to produce. What the Windward Marches required above all else was time undisturbed, and in a matter of days it received that rare gift. The effects were not spectacular. They were, instead, durable. The capacity built in the Windward Marches during this period would prove, in the crises that followed, to be neither excess nor luxury — only the margin that made recovery possible.

entries.expanded_text: The chronicles of the Tordun record the season the granaries reopened with the same gravity others reserve for battles won. Conditions across the Tordun steadied to dangerously unstable levels — not the prosperity anyone had hoped for, but a foundation solid enough to build upon, and after what had come before, no one complained. Stability returned to the Tordun, but it was the wary kind — the stability of people who had seen how quickly the ground could shift, and who slept lightly because of it.

entries.expanded_text: What befell the Calden, held by the Twin Banners in those years was not a single catastrophe but a sequence of failures, each compounding the last beyond recovery. Across the Calden, the population that survived the crisis emerged into circumstances so diminished that the distinction between endurance and defeat became largely academic. With stability at uneasy levels and the old structures in ruin, the Calden entered a period that later writers would describe only by what it lacked.
